records.sourceFile: Undeclared doping substances are highly prevalent in commercial sports nutrition supplements.pdf

paper.citation: Duiven E, van Loon LJC, Spruijt L, Koert W, de Hon OM. Undeclared doping substances are highly prevalent in commercial sports nutrition supplements. J Sports Sci Med. 2021;20:328-338.
paper.abstract: Sixty-six high-risk sports nutrition supplements bought from Dutch web shops were analysed for doping substances by an accredited anti-doping laboratory. Undeclared doping substances were found in 25 products (38%), with high levels of synthetic stimulants in three.
paper.tldr: More than a third of the high-risk sports nutrition supplements tested had doping substances that were not on the label. Athletes subject to testing should treat unlabelled contents as a real risk.
paper.methods: Products with hormone, muscle gain, fat loss or energy claims were selected from 21 brands and 17 web shops and bought in December 2014. Samples were screened by LGC with high-level and low-level GC-MS and LC-MS screens, with concentrations estimated by standard addition for high-level findings. Estimated maximum intakes were compared with WADA reporting levels and prescribed medicine doses.
paper.findings: Twenty-five products (38%) tested positive, 38 negative and three were inconclusive. Three products contained high levels of synthetic stimulants (oxilofrine, BMPEA, NBDMPEA) and the authors estimate that they could impose general health risks at the recommended dose. The most frequent low-level findings were the steroid boldione (11), the steroid 17alpha-AED and the stimulant 4-methylhexan-2-amine (DMAA) (6 each), and higenamine (4), for which WADA later set a reporting level.
paper.limitations: Purchases were made in 2014 and the sample was a preselected high-risk subset. Low-level findings were not quantified, and maximum intakes were estimated from assumed doses and reference medicines. Trend claims against earlier surveys rest on data not shown.
paper.practicalImplications: Supplements bought online with performance claims carry a real chance of undeclared substances. Athletes subject to doping control should discuss any product with the team medical staff before use and treat unlabelled contents as a possible positive test.
paper.athleteDev: Give athletes a clear rule that performance-claim supplements can contain undeclared stimulants or steroids, and screen any product with staff before use.
paper.rtp: The study covers contamination and doping risk and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Utility of Body Weight, Urine Color, and Thirst Perception (WUT) in Determining Hydration in Young Adults.pdf

paper.citation: Adams WM, Anderson T, Zaplatosch ME, Cheuvront SN, Kenefick R, Yates B, et al. Utility of Body Weight, Urine Color, and Thirst Perception (WUT) in Determining Hydration in Young Adults. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2024 (published ahead of print).
paper.abstract: The authors tested the body weight, urine color and thirst (WUT) hydration framework in 93 young adults. Using reference change values and a 2-hour passive heating and fluid manipulation protocol, they found that body mass change and thirst were the most important predictors of dehydration, and they proposed a weighted version of the WUT model.
paper.tldr: In healthy young adults, a change in morning body mass or thirst was the strongest signal of dehydration, with urine color adding less. A weighted WUT model may help people judge whether they need more fluid, but it has not been tested in athletes.
paper.methods: Phase 1 collected 24-hour and first-morning urine, body mass and thirst ratings over 3 days (Study 1, n = 58) or 7 days (Study 2, n = 35) of free-living life. Reference change values were computed for each WUT component. In Study 2, participants then completed a 2-hour seated passive heat exposure (40 C, 50% relative humidity) and were randomised to control, sweat-loss or fluid-restriction conditions, with dehydration probability compared by ANOVA and ridge regression used to weight the components.
paper.findings: After the manipulation, body mass change (-0.0%, -1.19%, -1.49% in control, sweat-loss and restriction) and thirst separated the groups for predicted dehydration probability (p = 0.001 and p < 0.001). For urine color the overall test was significant (p = 0.044), but only restriction differed from control (p = 0.047). Ridge regression explained 83% of variance, with body mass 58%, thirst 26% and the body mass by urine color and body mass by thirst interactions 5% each. The authors report that a body mass change of about 1% was more likely or very likely to indicate dehydration, and a 1-unit thirst change gave a 90% probability.
paper.limitations: Participants were healthy young adults who exercised 10 hours a week or less, so the reference values and weights may not apply to athletes, older adults or patients. Adherence to the fluid restriction was not verified and no participant was excluded, the regression used all data without a validation split, and the authors call for confirmation of the coefficients in other populations. The fluid manipulation involved only the 35 Study 2 participants split across three groups, and the reported 95% CI for the sweat-loss vs control difference (-0.11 to 0.57) crosses zero despite p = 0.003.
paper.practicalImplications: Use morning body mass change and first-morning thirst as the main day-to-day checks for fluid adequacy, with urine color as a supporting measure. Treat a body mass change above about 1% of normal body mass as a cue to drink more, consistent with the authors' recommendation.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The model could give athletes and staff a simple daily hydration check before training or competition. It was tested in healthy non-athletes who did not train heavily, so applying it to athletes needs its own validation before it guides fluid plans.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study does not include injured or recovering athletes and does not address return-to-play decisions. It cannot be used to judge fluid status during rehabilitation or return to play.

records.sourceFile: Vitamin D and the Athlete- Current                        Perspectives and New Challenges.pdf

paper.citation: Owens DJ, Allison R, Close GL. Vitamin D and the Athlete: Current Perspectives and New Challenges. Sports Med. 2018;48(Suppl 1):S3-S16.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of vitamin D in athletes, covering bone, muscle and immune roles, high-dose supplement risks, and paradoxes in Black athletes with low serum levels.
paper.tldr: Serum vitamin D has not clearly tracked bone health in athletes, and very high supplement doses may be harmful. Thresholds may need rethinking for ethnically diverse athletes, using bioavailable vitamin D.
paper.methods: Narrative review by the authors covering vitamin D history, biology, bone, muscle and immune function, supplementation, toxicity and ethnicity. No systematic search is described.
paper.findings: Serum 25(OH)D has consistently failed to show a clear relationship with bone health in athletes, which may partly reflect the osteogenic effect of exercise. Vitamin D may affect recovery from damaging exercise and infection risk, and the authors' group found smaller cardiac dimensions in severely deficient athletes. The authors say data from their laboratory suggest high-dose supplementation could be problematic, and Black athletes can have low serum 25(OH)D without clear physiological consequences.
paper.limitations: Narrative review without a described search, so evidence selection is not transparent. The review includes the authors' own laboratory data, and the article is part of an expert panel supplement with a disclosed honorarium from a PepsiCo division.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not assume more vitamin D is better; the authors advise against blanket supplementation, mega doses and bolus doses in favor of an individualized decision based on status. Routine screening may be unnecessary in the absence of pathology, and where testing is warranted the authors prefer bioavailable vitamin D over total serum 25(OH)D.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The authors state vitamin D is not an ergogenic aid, so supplementation above sufficiency should not be expected to improve performance. Very high doses deserve caution because 70,000 IU per week raised a catabolite that may counteract vitamin D signaling; muscle and immune benefits rest mostly on mechanistic, observational or small trial data.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review does not evaluate return-to-play decisions or injury recovery and should not be used to guide them.
